questions.question: What are the SOLID principles?
questions.title: The SOLID Principles
questions.direct_answer: SOLID is five OO design principles: Single Responsibility (a class has one reason to change), Open/Closed (open for extension, closed for modification — add behavior without editing), Liskov Substitution (a subclass can replace its parent without breaking), Interface Segregation (many small interfaces beat one fat one — don't force unused methods), Dependency Inversion (depend on abstractions, not concretions — inject dependencies). Together they aim for code that's easy to change and extend without breaking. They're guidelines, not laws; in Ruby (duck-typed, modules) they show up as small focused classes, modules over inheritance, and dependency injection.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can name the five SOLID principles and their one-line meaning, and know they're guidelines for changeable code.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating SOLID as laws (over-engineering) or only knowing the acronym without the meaning.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: SOLID = SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, DIP. SRP: one reason to change. OCP: extend, don't edit. LSP: subclass replaces parent. ISP: small interfaces. DIP: depend on abstractions.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: SOLID is five OO design principles. Single Responsibility: a class has one reason to change. Open/Closed: open for extension, closed for modification — add behavior without editing existing code. Liskov Substitution: a subclass can replace its parent without breaking the program. Interface Segregation: many small interfaces beat one fat one — don't force clients to depend on methods they don't use. Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions, not concretions — inject dependencies. Together they aim for code that's easy to change and extend without breaking. They're guidelines, not laws; in Ruby, with its duck typing and modules, they show up as small focused classes, modules over inheritance, and dependency injection rather than rigid interface hierarchies. A common mistake is treating SOLID as laws and over-engineering, and knowing only the acronym without the one-line meaning of each.

sections.title: SOLID in Ruby
sections.content:
```ruby
# SRP: a class does one thing
class InvoiceExporter
  def export(invoice); to_pdf(invoice); end  # only exporting
  private
def to_pdf(i); # ...
end
end
# (formatting lives in InvoiceFormatter, not here)

# DIP: depend on an abstraction (inject the logger)
class OrderProcessor
  def initialize(logger: Logger.new)   # inject, don't hardcode
    @logger = logger
  end
  def process(order); @logger.info('processing'); end
end

# OCP: extend without editing (a subclass or module adds behavior)
class PdfExporter < InvoiceExporter; def export(i); add_header; super; end; end
```
